Bagging

    Bagging & Random Forests

    From one parcel to a forest

    A parcel arrives at the sorting desk. Two trees disagree on where it should go. We’ll work out where that disagreement comes from, combine their answers, and check whether a forest works better on the next shipment.

    1. Ensemble modelsHear two trees answer the same question and see four ways to combine models.
    2. Bagging and Random Forest intuitionDraw the training trays, trace the trees, and see why averaging can steady a prediction.
    3. Random Forest implementationCheck the data, fit the baseline models, and read the tuning curves.
    4. Randomized SearchCompare a full grid with a fixed search budget on the same folds.
    5. Out-of-bag pointsScore a parcel using the trees that left it out of training.
    6. Interview questionsExplain feature importance, bias and variance, and when a branch earns its place.
    Start at the parcel desk

    Bagging & Random Forests

    Where should this parcel go?

    Imagine you run a courier sorting center. Routine parcels should move quickly. Some need a closer check.

    Past records pair the measurements with the route the courier took.

    What counts as unusual?

    In this example, a person checks the parcel if the barcode still won’t scan after a retry or it weighs over 1 kg more than the shipping label says. For example, a 5.2 kg parcel labeled 4 kg goes to Review, even if its barcode scans.

    Our training table keeps the measured weight, a scanner warning score from 0 to 10, and the route taken. Higher scores mean stronger warnings. The desk staff can also see the barcode flag and shipping-label weight. The trees use just the measured weight and scan score.

    Look at scan score alone. P5 scored 7.0 and went to Review. P3 scored 7.8 and went to Auto. A rule that reviews everything above one score would send P3 to Review whenever it sends P5 there. Each tree works from the examples it sees and can split on either input.

    Ensemble intuition

    Same parcel. Two trees.

    Give the parcel’s weight and scan score to two trees. Each tree learned from a different selection of the courier’s past records. Both used the same training settings, so look at how the examples they saw changed the cutoff they learned.

    ● Auto◆ Review⊕ New parcel

    Find the new parcel. Which side of each cut does it fall on?

    How to read the plots

    Each circle or diamond is a parcel from the past records. Its position shows weight and scan score, and its color shows the route the courier took.

    The line shows the first cutoff each tree learned. Find the new parcel marked with a plus and see which side it lands on. Reveal the calls to see which route the tree predicts in each shaded region.

    Follow the cut. The parcel’s scan score is 5.7. That’s below Tree 1’s cutoff of 5.8, so it reaches Auto. It’s above Tree 2’s cutoff of 5.25, so it reaches Review.

    One tree says Auto. The other says Review. The courier still needs one route, so we can ask several models for their predictions and use a rule, such as a vote, to make the final call.

    That group of models and its rule make an ensemble. Each model that contributes an answer is a base learner. Here each tree is a base learner.

    Bagging

    Give each tree its own sample drawn from the courier’s records. Train the trees separately, then combine their predictions for the new parcel.

    Boosting

    Build the trees in order. In gradient-boosted decision trees (GBDT), each new tree learns a correction to the current model. If the model keeps missing parcels that need Review, the next tree can learn a pattern that helps correct those predictions.

    Stacking

    Give a second model the first models’ predictions as inputs. For example, it can learn how to combine a decision tree’s answer with a logistic regression model’s answer for each parcel.

    Cascading

    Send parcels through models in stages. A quick first model can route a clear case immediately. If a parcel is borderline, pass it to a second model with more measurements for a closer decision.

    What changed between the two trees?

    When a tree compares possible cutoffs, it counts the Auto and Review rows on each side. A new sample can repeat some rows and leave others out. That changes the counts, so a different cutoff can work better for that tree.

    How does stacking get examples for the second model?

    Set aside a group of past parcels. Train the first models on the rest, then ask them to predict that group. The second model learns from those predictions and the group’s recorded routes. Rotating which group we set aside gives us predictions for more parcels. These are called out-of-fold predictions.

    Quiz 1

    Where did the two training samples come from?

    Draw a training sample

    Bagging

    Draw a bootstrap sample

    The courier has 12 past parcel records. We want to give each tree its own training sample. How can we do that with the same 12 records?

    Bootstrap · Fill one tray per tree

    Make 12 draws from the original pile. Since every ticket goes back, you might copy P2 twice and miss another parcel entirely. That new tray of 12 draws is one bootstrap sample. Start again from the same original pile for the next tree.

    Aggregate · Combine the trees’ answers

    Train each tree on its own tray. A different mix of records can change the questions a tree learns. Then give every tree the same new parcel. If two trees say Review and one says Auto, a majority vote gives Review. Combining the answers is aggregation.

    Bagging is short for bootstrap aggregating. Make a training sample for each model, then combine their predictions so the final route depends on several models.

    Draw from the parcel desk

    Choose Tree 1 and click Draw next parcel twice. Watch the ID and its count.

      Quiz 2

      1. Draw a whole row. P2 carries its weight (2.0), scan score (5.0), and recorded route (Auto) together. The measurements are features. The route is the label the tree learns to predict.
      2. Put it back. The first two draws for Tree 1 both select P2. Each copy carries the same measurements and the same Auto label.
      3. Compare the trays. Use Show all draws to count Tree 1’s repeated and omitted IDs. Then select Tree 2 and do the same. The original table stays the same while the mix in each tray changes.
      Check your count for Tree 1

      Tree 1 takes 12 draws and sees 8 distinct parcels. P2 appears three times, so its Auto label contributes three times to that tree’s training counts. P3, P4, P7, and P11 each appear zero times. Those four rows are out of bag for Tree 1. Check Tree 2 to see that P7 can appear in another sample.

      What changes without replacement?

      With 12 draws from 12 rows and no replacement, every row appears once. Drawing fewer than 12 without replacement would give a subset with no repeats. With replacement, repeated and omitted rows can occur even when the number of draws equals the original row count.

      How do we combine the predictions?

      For classification, one simple approach is to count the predicted classes and choose the majority. Another approach averages probabilities by class. For numerical regression, average the predicted numbers.

      We have three different samples. Give each one to its own tree and follow the same new parcel through all three.

      Random Forest intuition

      Train three trees and combine their answers

      Each tray holds a different mix of the courier’s past parcels. Give one tray to each tree and let it learn which questions separate Auto from Review. When the new parcel arrives, give all three trees its same measurements and see whether they agree.

      1. Sample. Make a tray of 12 draws for each tree. Each time you pick a row, keep a copy in the tray and allow the original to be picked again.
      2. Fit. Train each tree on its own tray. It uses the recorded routes to choose questions such as “Is the scan score at most 5.8?”
      3. Predict. Give each trained tree the same 5.65 kg parcel with a scan score of 5.7. Answer its questions until you reach a leaf, the group where that tree makes its prediction.
      4. Combine. Each tree can vote Auto or Review. We can also average the Review probabilities from the three leaves. Either rule gives the courier one final route.

      Run the core code

      Change the sampling line, fit one tree, and predict the same parcel. Then run the cell that fits all three trees.

      Open intuition notebook
      rng = np.random.default_rng(bootstrap_seed)
draw = rng.choice(len(X), size=len(X), replace=True)
tree = DecisionTreeClassifier(criterion='gini', max_depth=2, random_state=tree_seed)
tree.fit(X.iloc[draw], y.iloc[draw])
tree.predict(parcel)
      Walk through the code line by line
      1. Set the seed. The bootstrap seed is 11. Start a fresh generator with that seed to replay the same draws.
      2. Draw row positions. len(X) is 12, so the positions run from 0 to 11. size=len(X) asks for 12 draws. replace=True makes each position eligible again. The first positions are 1, 1, and 9, which correspond to P2, P2, and P10.
      3. Set up the tree. Gini measures how mixed the labels are. The tree looks for splits that make the child groups less mixed. max_depth=2 allows up to two questions on a path to a leaf. The tree seed of 0 controls random choices during fitting.
      4. Fit the tree. X holds the measurements and y holds the recorded routes. Use iloc[draw] on both so every parcel stays paired with its own route. If P2 is drawn twice, both its measurements and its Auto label enter the training sample twice.
      5. Predict the new parcel. tree.predict(parcel) takes its weight and scan score. The tree applies the questions it learned and returns Auto or Review.

      In the notebook, try replace=False and count how many different rows you get in 12 draws. Restore True and rerun from the seed to get the sample shown here.

      Expected output and what to point at

      Read the sample IDs first, then the tree prediction. This small hand-built ensemble makes the bootstrap and aggregation visible. The second notebook adds the full scikit-learn Random Forest workflow.

      Follow the parcel through each tree

      Start with Tree 1. Compare the parcel’s scan score of 5.7 with the first cutoff. Then switch to Tree 2 and make the same comparison.

      Quiz 3

      Work through the three routes and both final answers

      Tree 1. 5.7 is at most 5.8. The Yes leaf has 8 Auto and 0 Review occurrences, so the tree says Auto.

      Tree 2. 5.7 is greater than 5.25. The No leaf has 0 Auto and 7 Review occurrences, so the tree says Review.

      Tree 3. The parcel’s weight of 5.65 takes the Yes branch at 7.25. Its scan score then takes the No branch at 5.25. That leaf has 1 Auto and 2 Review occurrences, so the tree says Review.

      Hard vote. Two of three trees say Review, for a Review vote share of 66.7%.

      Probability average. The Review shares inside the reached leaves are 0/8, 7/7, and 2/3. Their average is 5/9, or 55.6%. That also gives Review the larger share for this parcel.

      Is vote share the same as average predicted probability?

      Each hard vote contributes one class. In a probability average, a leaf with two Review rows and one Auto row contributes a Review probability of 2/3. For example, three Review probabilities of 0.49, 0.49 and 0.99 give two Auto hard votes but a mean Review probability of about 0.657. In scikit-learn, the forest classifier picks the class with the largest mean probability.

      Scikit-learn probability reference

      What if the courier needs an estimate in minutes?

      Suppose the target is now minutes until dispatch. We train three regression trees on records that include the actual time. Each tree gives a number for the same new parcel.

      Tree 19 minutes
      Tree 211 minutes
      Tree 313 minutes

      The Random Forest regression prediction is their mean, (9 + 11 + 13) ÷ 3 = 11 minutes.

      Scikit-learn regression prediction reference

      Changing the training rows gave us three different trees. A Random Forest also samples which features a tree can consider at each split. Let’s see what happens if the tree can ask about weight for one question and scan score for the next.

      How do we get different trees?

      Change the rows and the candidate features

      Imagine scan score wins the first question in tree after tree. Even with different samples, those trees could learn similar rules. A Random Forest adds another draw. Each tree gets its own sample of parcels, and each split gets a fresh list of feature columns to consider.

      1. Which parcels does this tree learn from? Give it a bootstrap sample. When a parcel is drawn twice, its label counts twice as the tree learns.
      2. Which measurements can it ask about here? If the first split draws Weight, it can try weight cutoffs. At the next split, a fresh draw could bring in Scan score.
      3. Which question separates the labels best? The tree tests questions on the parcels that reached this node. It chooses the allowed question that reduces the mix of Auto and Review labels the most.

      A different candidate list at each node

      Use the rows in Tree 2’s sample. The root is its first question. The Yes child holds the parcels that answered Yes to the original root question.

      Quiz 4

      Try it. Start with Both features and read the best question at the root. Click Reveal next feature draw. Which question can the root choose when only Weight is offered? Which feature is offered to the Yes child?

      Check the first feature draw

      With both features available, the root picks Scan score ≤ 5.25 for a Gini decrease of 0.3111. The first one-feature draw offers only Weight at the root, where Weight ≤ 3 gives a decrease of 0.2963. It offers Scan score at the fixed Yes child, where Scan score ≤ 3.75 gives a decrease of 0.0533.

      We keep the rows in these two cards fixed while we change the candidate list. When a forest grows a tree, a different first question can also change which parcels reach the Yes child.

      Draw parcels for each tree. Draw feature columns for each split. If weight is the only option at one root, that tree has a chance to learn a rule another tree would have skipped. Different rules can help the forest catch mistakes that several similar trees would share.
      Does choosing fewer features always help?

      A shorter list gives the tree a chance to use a different measurement. It can also leave out a strong feature that would have separated Auto and Review better. Try several list sizes and check which one predicts better on validation data.

      Where does the 0.3111 Gini decrease come from?

      Gini measures how mixed the Auto and Review labels are at a node. The root has four Auto and eight Review draws, so its Gini is 1 − (4/12)² − (8/12)² ≈ 0.4444. The scan cut leaves four Auto and one Review in the Yes group and seven Review in the No group. Their Gini scores are 0.32 and 0, weighted by 5/12 and 7/12. Subtracting that weighted result from the root score gives 0.4444 − [(5/12 × 0.32) + (7/12 × 0)] ≈ 0.3111.

      We’ve made the trees different. Now let’s see how much we want each one to learn.

      Properties of base learners

      Useful alone, better able to disagree

      Tree 3 can ask about weight first, then ask about scan score on just one branch. That lets it learn a pattern that uses both measurements. Each tree is a base learner, an individual model that contributes an answer. When useful trees make different mistakes, combining their answers can give us a steadier decision.

      When a tree is too simple

      A tree with one question can miss a real pattern that depends on both weight and scan score. When the same pattern is missed across many new training samples, the model is underfitting and can have high bias.

      When a tree learns its tray too well

      A deep tree can capture that pattern and also learn a cutoff that matches a few unusual training tickets. Overfitting happens when fitting those details hurts predictions on new parcels. Flexible trees can reduce bias and become more sensitive to which rows they saw, increasing variance.

      Change the maximum depth

      Maximum depth sets how many questions a parcel can answer on its way to the tree’s decision. All three trees refit on their original samples so you can see what changing the limit does.

      The diagram shows Tree 1. Each card shows its own tree’s answer for the new parcel and how many of its training draws it got right. A parcel drawn twice counts twice in that training total.

      Try it. Change depth from 1 to 2 and watch Tree 3. Its second question helps it get 11 of 12 training draws right, up from 10 of 12. It also changes its answer for our new parcel from Auto to Review. To judge whether the extra question helps with new parcels, test it on a separate group the tree hasn’t seen.

      How much should one tree learn?

      At depth 0 the tree makes the same call for every parcel. It picks whichever route appears more often in its sample. At depth 2 it can learn an interaction, where the value of one feature changes how another feature is used. For instance, it can ask about scan score for just the lighter parcels. Extra questions can also pick up patterns that were peculiar to this tray. Averaging several trees helps when those details send the individual predictions in different directions.

      What if every tree makes the same mistake?

      Every vote points the same way, so the aggregate makes that same mistake. For a numerical prediction, averaging identical numbers also leaves the prediction unchanged.

      Keep the new parcel fixed and change the training batch. How much does the answer move when we use one tree or an average of trees?

      Variance

      Why averaging steadies a prediction

      Imagine we train one tree on a batch of past parcel records, then start over with a fresh batch. We give both trees the same new parcel. A different mix of training rows can change the first split, where the parcel lands, and the chance of Review the tree assigns.

      Model variance measures how spread out those predictions are across training runs. In each batch, we’ll also train several trees and average their Review probabilities for that parcel. We can then compare how far the single-tree prediction and the average move from batch to batch.

      1. Keep the parcel fixed. Its weight, scan score and true route stay the same.
      2. Refit both models. Train one tree on the batch. To build the ensemble, draw several bootstrap samples from that same batch and train one tree per sample.
      3. Compare the spread. Look at the Review probability across batches for each model.

      What changes if one training label changes?

      Freeze the three bootstrap trays and the new parcel. Then flip P3’s recorded route from Auto to Review and refit. Check which trees actually saw P3.

      Trays that omitted P3 are unchanged. A tray that included P3 can learn a different rule or leaf probability. In a bigger forest, a row may appear in many trays.

      Same parcel, five new training batches

      Each row is one training run. Its two dots show the chance of Review for the same parcel, on a scale from 0 to 1. Reveal a second row and compare how far each dot moves. The probabilities here are illustrative.

      Work out the spread for the first two batches

      Reveal Batch B. The single tree gives Review probabilities of 0.10 and 0.90. Their mean is 0.50. Both estimates are 0.40 away from that mean, so their mean squared distance is 0.16.

      The bagged trees give 0.42 and 0.56. Their mean is 0.49. Both estimates are 0.07 away, so their mean squared distance is 0.0049. The square roots, 0.40 and 0.07, are the standard deviations shown as spread.

      Across all five batches, both sets of predictions average 0.50. The bagged predictions sit closer to that average. A steady prediction can still be wrong. If the parcel’s recorded route is Auto and a model always predicts an 80% chance of Review, a 50% cutoff gives the wrong route every time. To measure accuracy, compare predicted routes with recorded routes on held-out parcels.

      What if the trees move together?

      Suppose one tree’s Review estimate rises 10 percentage points from its usual value and another’s falls 10 points. The changes cancel in the average. When both rise 10 points, their average rises by 10 points too.

      One tree
      Average of trees

      Shared part Part that shrinks

      Pairwise correlation describes how much two trees’ predictions tend to move together across training runs. On this scale, 0 means their changes have no linear relationship, and 1 means they move in perfect step. The bar treats each tree as equally variable and gives every pair the same correlation.

      Start with 10 trees and correlation 0.30. Take one tree’s variance as 100%. The shared 30% stays in the average. Averaging 10 trees divides the remaining 70% by 10, leaving 7%. Together, that is 37% of one tree’s variance. Increase to 100 trees and the ratio falls to 30.7%.

      Derive the variance of the average

      Let B be the number of trees, σ² the variance of each prediction, and ρ the pairwise correlation. The variance of a sum has B variance terms and B(B − 1) ordered covariance terms. Each covariance is ρσ². Dividing by B² for the average gives

      Var(average) = [Bσ² + B(B − 1)ρσ²] / B² = σ²[ρ + (1 − ρ)/B]

      With three trees, each prediction pairs with itself once, giving three variance terms. The distinct pairs are trees 1 and 2, 1 and 3, and 2 and 3. The sum expansion counts each pair in both orders, giving six covariance terms. That is why three trees give [3σ² + 6ρσ²] / 9.

      Set correlation to 0 to see the uncorrelated case. Set it to 1 to see perfectly correlated predictions. Positive correlation leaves a shared part of the variance as the number of trees grows.

      Why sample features?

      A strong feature can dominate many trees. Giving a node a smaller candidate set lets different useful splits emerge, which can reduce how closely the trees move together.

      Can a stable prediction still be biased?

      Suppose heavier parcels with a high scan score need review far more often than other parcels. Trees that can ask only one question may keep underestimating Review for that group. If the average prediction across fresh training batches is still too low, that systematic error is bias. Adding trees can make the average steadier while leaving that error in place.

      Where do bias, variance, and noise show up in squared error?

      At a fixed parcel, average the squared prediction error over fresh training sets and possible dispatch times. When the new outcome is independent of the training draw, the expected error has three components.

      Expected squared error = bias² + prediction variance + irreducible noise.

      Bias² · 1 min²

      Across two equally likely training samples, the model predicts 12 or 16 minutes. The mean prediction is 14. The true mean is 13, so the squared gap is (14 − 13)².

      Variance · 4 min²

      Both predictions are 2 minutes from their own mean of 14. The average squared distance is 4.

      Noise · 9 min²

      For identical measured inputs, actual dispatch takes 10 or 16 minutes with equal probability. Both are 3 minutes away from the true mean of 13.

      These parts sum to 14 min². Averaging can shrink the variance part. A systematic prediction gap or unpredictable dispatch delay can still remain.

      The model has two jobs now. Grow individual trees and combine their predictions. Put both into a reproducible training workflow.

      Random Forest code implementation

      Fit, tune, and evaluate a forest

      The courier wants a forest it can use on tomorrow’s parcels. Which settings should it pick? Tuning means comparing choices such as tree depth and feature-list size. We select those settings using one group of past parcels and save a separate group for the final check.

      From parcel records to a fair comparison

      The implementation notebook uses 1,400 original synthetic records. It adds seal quality, handling steps, fragility, and a noise column to weight and scan score.

      Open implementation notebook
      1. Inspect the records. Check column types, missing values, duplicate records and parcel IDs. Use the ID to track a row. Use the parcel measurements to predict its route.
      2. Reserve 350 test parcels. A stratified split keeps roughly the same route proportions. Use the other 1,050 parcels for all fitting and tuning.
      3. Fit a baseline tree and forest. Compare both on the same measurements and splits. Their scores give us a reference for what tuning achieves.
      4. Rotate four validation folds. Fit on three folds and score the fourth, then rotate. Compare settings by their mean validation score.

      Change one forest setting at a time

      Start with tree depth. Watch what happens to the score on training folds and the score on validation folds as the trees can ask more questions. Then try changing the number of trees, the feature budget, and the two limits on node size.

      These are seeded notebook results from scikit-learn 1.6.1. In the score table, validation refers to the rotating folds within the training set. The final test parcels are still set aside.

      Is the parent big enough to try?

      min_samples_split checks the parent before a split. A node with 10 rows qualifies at a minimum of 8. At a minimum of 11, it stays a leaf.

      Would both children be big enough?

      min_samples_leaf checks each proposed child. With a minimum of 3, a 9 | 1 split is ruled out while a 6 | 4 split clears that requirement.

      Which other settings can I change?

      criterion changes how a split is scored. max_leaf_nodes caps leaves, min_weight_fraction_leaf sets a minimum share of sample weight per leaf, and min_impurity_decrease requires a minimum weighted impurity drop. The search ranges should reflect the data size and the job the model has to do.

      Run a small grid search

      Pair two depth limits with two feature budgets. Each of the four pairings is fitted four times, once per validation fold. Use the settings from the prepared notebook.

      small_space = {'max_depth': [2, 4], 'max_features': [1, 'sqrt']}
grid_demo = GridSearchCV(
    tuning_base, small_space, cv=folds,
    scoring='balanced_accuracy', refit=False
).fit(X_train, y_train)

      Compare the mean validation scores in grid_demo.cv_results_. This demonstration stops after scoring the four combinations. The full tuning run refits the winner.

      Why balanced accuracy?

      Suppose 90 of 100 parcels are Auto. Sending every parcel to Auto would give 90% accuracy and miss every Review. Balanced accuracy finds the fraction correct within each actual route and averages those fractions. Here it averages 100% for Auto and 0% for Review, giving 50%.

      We can read the effect of one setting. Next, look at how two search strategies try combinations.

      Compare the search strategies

      Hyperparameter search

      Randomized Search

      Suppose the courier wants to test two depth limits and two feature budgets. There are four possible pairings. If time is tight, what can we learn from trying just two?

      Same candidates, different search budgets

      Grid search checks every pairing in the grid. Randomized search samples a fixed number of configurations. Compare them using the same candidate pool, four folds, forest seed, and balanced accuracy.

      A grid sees the best score among all pairings in its grid. A randomized search can miss it, and it can cover a much larger space when fitting every pairing is impractical. The best validation score still needs a separate test.

      Run the broader search and read the final test

      The notebook also samples 15 configurations from a larger space. Each is fitted on four folds, for 60 search fits before the winner is refit.

      search = RandomizedSearchCV(
    RandomForestClassifier(bootstrap=True, oob_score=True, random_state=seed),
    parameter_space, n_iter=15, scoring='balanced_accuracy',
    cv=folds, refit=True, random_state=seed
)
search.fit(X_train, y_train)
forest = search.best_estimator_
test_predictions = forest.predict(X_test)

      parameter_space gives the choices or distributions. The search seed replays the configuration draws. The forest seed controls randomness within a fit.

      Read the two scores. Use 81.26% to see how the winning setting did on average during its four cross-validation checks. Then use 78.88% to see how the refitted forest did on the 350 parcels reserved for the final test. Both use balanced accuracy.

      Read the worked notebook results

      With 1,050 training rows and 350 held-out rows, the selected candidate averaged 81.26% balanced accuracy across four validation folds. The held-out balanced accuracies were 72.65% for the single tree, 76.89% for the baseline forest, and 78.88% for the tuned forest. The tuned forest’s OOB accuracy was 81.24% across 1,050 covered training rows. That last value uses ordinary accuracy on the OOB predictions. Results are from the seeded run with scikit-learn 1.6.1.

      Read the per-class report

      The tuned forest flagged 151 parcels for Review. Of those, 110 really needed Review. That gives precision = 110 ÷ 151 ≈ 72.8%. There were 142 actual Review parcels, so recall = 110 ÷ 142 ≈ 77.5%. F1 is the harmonic mean of those two rates, 220 ÷ 293 ≈ 75.1%. The report’s support is the 142 actual Review parcels. Read the Auto row the same way with Auto as the class of interest.

      The forest also has a way to check parcels that never entered a particular tree’s training tray. Let’s see which trees can give us that check.

      Out-of-bag scoring

      Which trees can evaluate this parcel?

      Look for the ticket for parcel O1 in three training trays. Trees 1 and 2 drew it zero times, so they learned their splits using other parcels. We can ask those two trees to predict O1’s route, then compare their joint answer with the route the courier recorded.

      We say that O1 is out of bag (OOB) for Trees 1 and 2. The “bag” is one tree’s bootstrap sample. O1 appears in Tree 3’s tray, so Tree 3 is left out of this check. Another parcel may have a different group of trees available.

      Pick a training parcel

      This five-parcel example has three trees. Each draws five rows with replacement and learns one split on weight.

      Times each parcel was drawn into each tree's bootstrap sample
      ParcelWeightTrue labelTree 1Tree 2Tree 3

      Read across a row to see how often each tree drew that parcel. A 2× means the tree trained on two copies. A zero means that tree can take part in the OOB check.

      1. Find the zeros. Try O1. Only Trees 1 and 2 left it out of their training trays.
      2. Read the leaves. Follow that parcel's weight through each eligible tree. Average the fractions of Review draws in those leaves.
      3. Check the route. For O1, the two Review fractions are 1/3 and 0/2. Their mean is about 16.7%, so the combined answer is Auto. That matches O1’s recorded label. Then try O2, whose ticket appears in every tray.
      See the samples and their learned cuts

      From one parcel to the OOB score

      Do the same check for every parcel. First count how many parcels got an OOB prediction. Then, among that group, count how many predicted routes match the recorded routes.

      Reveal all OOB predictions

      Coverage asks which parcels we could score. O1, O3 and O4 have eligible predictions, so coverage is 3 out of 5.

      Accuracy asks how many of those predictions match. O1 and O4 match. O3 was recorded as Review, and its OOB prediction is Auto. That gives 2 correct out of 3 scored parcels, or about 66.7%.

      Classification error asks how many are wrong. On the same scored parcels, OOB error is 1 − 2/3 = 1/3 ≈ 33.3%. The two parcels without an OOB prediction count toward coverage only.

      Why roughly 37%?

      With n training rows, one uniform draw misses a particular row with probability 1 − 1/n. If a tree takes m independent draws with replacement, the chance it misses that row throughout is (1 − 1/n)m. When m equals n and n is large, this approaches e−1 ≈ 36.8%. Here, with five rows and five draws, the probability is about 32.8%.

      When is this score useful?

      OOB gives a convenient internal check when a bootstrapped forest already has trees that missed each row. Cross-validation can compare different models on shared folds. Reserve a separate held-out test set for final evaluation, especially after using OOB or cross-validation to choose settings. In scikit-learn Random Forest, enabling OOB scoring requires bootstrap sampling.

      What if every tree saw the parcel?

      There is no eligible OOB prediction for that parcel. This lab reports coverage and scores only rows with predictions. If every tree instead omitted the parcel, all of them would be eligible. The number of omitted rows in one tray is the original row count minus the number of distinct rows drawn.

      You can now read three views of the forest. The trees' individual decisions, their combined prediction, and an estimate of generalization. Connect those views to model settings and interview questions.

      Interview questions

      Explain importance and tune the trade-offs

      A colleague at the courier desk asks two questions. Which measurement did the forest rely on, and what would change if we gave each tree a different depth limit? Start by tracing how a split earns credit. Then pick a setting and explain what it would change about the forest.

      How does a forest compute feature importance?

      Every draw reaches the first split in Tree 2. Its later weight question affects just the parcels that reach that branch. Impurity-based feature importance gives a question more credit when it separates the labels well and reaches more rows.

      Multiply each split’s impurity decrease by the fraction of training draws that reached it. Credit the feature used at that split. Add the credits for each feature, express them as shares of that tree’s total, then average those shares across the trees.

      When a tree splits but never uses a feature, it contributes zero for that feature. Tree 1 uses only scan score, so its weight entry is 0%. The ensemble average keeps that zero in the denominator. Scikit-learn skips root-only trees in this calculation.

      Work through the numbers for these trees

      In Tree 2, the scan-score split is at the root, so all 12 draws reach it. Its weighted credit is 12/12 × 0.3111 ≈ 0.3111. The weight split is lower down. Its weighted credit is 5/12 × 0.32 ≈ 0.1333.

      Those credits total about 0.4444. Dividing each credit by that total gives 70% scan score and 30% weight within Tree 2. Across the three trees, mean weight importance is (0% + 30% + 64.3%) ÷ 3 ≈ 31.4%. The other 68.6% goes to scan score.

      A feature with many possible cutoffs gets more chances to earn split credit. For a check on fresh data, shuffle the scan scores among the held-out parcels, keep each parcel’s other information in place, and score the same forest again. The drop in score tells you how much this forest relied on scan score in that test. This is permutation importance.

      Five settings, five different changes

      Pick one setting. Imagine keeping the other four fixed, then say which part changes. Does it affect the training tray, the questions a tree can ask, or the number of predictions we combine?

      Why can more trees give diminishing returns?

      If several trees already tend to give the same parcel the same answer, another similar tree adds little new information. More trees can steady the average and also take longer to train and use. Compare how much each increase improves the validation score.

      How do depth and pruning differ?

      Maximum depth caps how many questions a parcel can answer while the tree grows. Pruning checks whether a branch earns its extra size by improving the separation of the labels. A larger ccp_alpha makes that size more costly, so simpler trees are favored. A simpler tree may vary less with the training sample and also miss a useful pattern.

      When does a branch earn its place?

      Consider two possible subtrees from a parcel model. The four-leaf subtree separates the training labels better, so it has lower weighted leaf impurity. Each extra leaf comes with a cost. Move the penalty slider and watch which subtree becomes cheaper.

      Cost = weighted leaf impurity + α × number of leaves. Weighted leaf impurity adds each leaf’s impurity multiplied by its share of training weight.

      These are two illustrative pruning candidates. Starting with a fitted tree, cost-complexity pruning considers simpler subtrees. max_depth constrains the questions while the tree grows.
